metadata.title: Synapse Study - Medical Immunology High-Yield Definitions & Questions

definitions.definition: Any substance that can specifically bind to an antigen receptor (such as TCR on T cells or BCR/antibodies on B cells) to induce an immune response.
properties: Immunogenicity: The ability to stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies or sensitized lymphocytes.
Immunoreactivity (Antigenicity): The ability to specifically bind to the generated antibodies or effector T cells.

definitions.definition: The specific, small chemical group or structural region (usually 5–15 amino acids) on an antigen molecule that directly binds to the antigen-binding site of a specific antibody, BCR, or TCR.
definitions.notes: It is the fundamental structural unit of antigen specificity.

definitions.definition: A linear peptide sequence (usually 8–24 amino acids) located inside the antigen molecule that must be processed and presented by Antigen-Presenting Cells (APCs) in complex with MHC molecules to be recognized by TCRs.
definitions.notes: Requires intracellular processing and MHC restriction.

definitions.definition: Conformational or linear chemical groups accessible on the external surface of native, intact antigens that bind directly to B-Cell Receptors (BCRs) or free soluble antibodies without requiring APC processing or MHC presentation.
definitions.notes: Recognizes native 3D conformational surfaces.

definitions.definition: A class of potent antigens (often bacterial exotoxins like Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 / TSST-1) that can polyclonally activate 2% to 20% of all peripheral T cells at extremely low concentrations without requiring intracellular processing by APCs.
definitions.notes: Binds directly to the outer surface of MHC Class II molecules and the Vβ domain of TCRs, triggering a massive 'cytokine storm'.

definitions.definition: A substance that has immunoreactivity (can bind specifically to pre-formed antibodies) but lacks immunogenicity on its own. It only becomes immunogenic when chemically coupled to a large carrier protein.
definitions.notes: Classic clinical example: Penicillin binding to albumin causing drug-induced hypersensitivity.

definitions.definition: A substance that possesses both immunogenicity (induces an immune response) and immunoreactivity (specifically binds to antibodies/effector lymphocytes).
definitions.notes: Usually large, complex foreign macromolecules like proteins or complex polysaccharides.

definitions.definition: A type of common antigen shared between completely unrelated biological species (animals, plants, humans, and microbes) without evolutionary kinship.
definitions.notes: Clinically important in serological diagnostic tests (e.g. Paul-Bunnell test for Infectious Mononucleosis / EBV).

definitions.definition: A non-specific immunostimulatory substance that, when injected together with an antigen or beforehand, non-specifically enhances the body's immune response to that antigen or alters the type of immune response.
definitions.notes: Examples: Aluminum hydroxide (Alum), Freund's complete adjuvant.

definitions.definition: A globular glycoprotein produced by activated B cells (plasma cells) in response to antigen stimulation that specifically binds to that antigen to execute protective biological functions.
definitions.notes: Consists of 2 Heavy (H) chains and 2 Light (L) chains joined by disulfide bonds into a Y-shaped structure.

definitions.definition: The immunological process where antibodies (especially IgG1 and IgG3) or complement fragments (C3b, C4b) coat the surface of a pathogen, allowing phagocytes (macrophages/neutrophils) with Fcγ receptors or complement receptors to easily bind, ingest, and destroy the invader.
definitions.notes: From Greek 'opsonion' — to prepare food / make tasty for eating.

definitions.definition: A cell-killing mechanism where low-affinity Fc receptors (such as CD16 / FcγRIII on Natural Killer cells, macrophages, or eosinophils) bind to the Fc portion of IgG antibodies that have already coated target cells (virus-infected cells, parasites, or tumors), triggering the release of perforin and granzymes to lyse the target.
definitions.notes: Non-specific killer cell targeted specifically by bound antibody.

definitions.definition: A polypeptide component synthesized by mucosal epithelial cells that wraps around dimeric Secretory IgA (sIgA) during transcytosis. It protects sIgA from degradation by gastrointestinal and proteolytic digestive enzymes in mucosal secretions.
definitions.notes: Essential for mucosal surface defense in saliva, tears, colostrum, and gut mucus.

definitions.definition: A heat-labile cascade system consisting of more than 30 soluble proteins, membrane-bound receptors, and regulatory proteins present in normal human and animal serum and tissue fluids. Once activated, it mediates cell lysis, opsonization, and inflammation.
definitions.notes: Activated via Classical, Alternative, or MBL Lectin pathways.

definitions.definition: The common terminal lytic structure (C5b-6-7-8-9n) assembled during the complement cascade that inserts itself into the target cell or bacterial membrane, creating a transmembrane pore that allows water and electrolytes to rush inside, causing rapid osmotic swelling and lysis.
definitions.notes: Target cell destroyed by osmotic lysis.

definitions.definition: Low-molecular-weight (8–30 kDa) soluble polypeptides secreted by activated immune and non-immune cells in response to stimuli. They act as messenger signaling proteins that mediate and regulate immunity, inflammation, and hematopoiesis.
definitions.notes: Acts via autocrine, paracrine, or endocrine routes with pleiotropy, redundancy, synergy, and antagonism.

definitions.definition: A specific family of cytokines secreted by virus-infected cells and immune cells that bind to neighboring cell receptors, inducing the expression of antiviral proteins (like 2',5'-oligoadenylate synthetase and protein kinase R) to block viral replication and spread.
definitions.notes: Type I: IFN-α, IFN-β (antiviral); Type II: IFN-γ (activates macrophages & Th1 response).

definitions.definition: An international nomenclature system used to identify, classify, and standardize cell surface molecules (differentiation antigens) expressed on leukocytes and other immune cells.
definitions.notes: Crucial for identifying cell lineages and functions (e.g. CD3 = all T cells, CD4 = Helper T, CD8 = Cytotoxic T, CD19/20 = B cells).

definitions.definition: Transmembrane cell surface proteins that mediate physical binding between cells (cell-cell interaction) or between cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM).
definitions.notes: Includes selectins, integrins, and the Ig superfamily. Essential for leukocyte rolling, extravasation, and lymphocyte homing.

definitions.definition: A tightly linked cluster of highly polymorphic genes (termed HLA in humans) that encode cell surface glycoproteins responsible for presenting processed peptide antigens to T lymphocytes.
definitions.notes: MHC Class I: All nucleated cells -> CD8+ T cells. MHC Class II: Professional APCs -> CD4+ T cells.

definitions.definition: A vital maturation checkpoint in the thymic cortex where developing double-positive (CD4+CD8+) thymocytes are tested for their ability to bind self-MHC molecules with low/moderate affinity. Cells that recognize self-MHC receive survival signals; those that cannot die by neglect (MHC Restriction).
definitions.notes: Outcome: Generates self-MHC restricted CD4+ or CD8+ single-positive T cells.

definitions.definition: A central tolerance checkpoint in the thymic medulla where thymocytes that bind to self-MHC/self-peptide complexes with excessively high affinity are induced to undergo apoptosis (clonal deletion) to prevent the emergence of autoreactive T cells.
definitions.notes: Outcome: Establishes central immune self-tolerance and prevents autoimmune disease.

definitions.definition: Specialized cells that capture, process, and display peptide antigens bound to MHC Class II molecules on their surface, along with essential co-stimulatory signals (like CD80/CD86), to activate naive T lymphocytes.
definitions.notes: Professional APCs: Dendritic cells (most potent), Macrophages, and B lymphocytes.

definitions.definition: The body's hard-wired, non-specific first line of defense present from birth. It responds immediately (0–4 hours) to infection using anatomical barriers, chemical mediators (complement, lysozyme), and phagocytes via Pattern Recognition Receptors without generating immunological memory.
definitions.notes: Includes physical barriers, neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, and complement.

definitions.definition: Germline-encoded receptors expressed on innate immune cells (macrophages, dendritic cells) that recognize evolutionary conserved microbial structures (PAMPs) and endogenous danger molecules (DAMPs).
definitions.notes: Key families: Toll-Like Receptors (TLRs), NOD-Like Receptors (NLRs), scavenger receptors.

definitions.definition: Conserved, invariant molecular signatures shared across large classes of microorganisms that are essential for their survival but are absent from host human cells.
definitions.notes: Examples: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS on Gram-negative bacteria), peptidoglycan, flagellin, unmethylated CpG DNA, and viral double-stranded RNA.

definitions.definition: The antigen-specific defense system mediated by clonal expansion and differentiation of T and B lymphocytes. It features exquisite specificity, diversity, self/non-self discrimination, and long-lasting immunological memory.
definitions.notes: Develops over days/weeks; secondary response is faster and stronger.

definitions.definition: The branch of adaptive immunity mediated specifically by T lymphocytes (CD4+ Helper T cells and CD8+ Cytotoxic T cells) without requiring antibodies. It eliminates intracellular pathogens (viruses, mycobacteria), parasites, and malignant tumor cells.
definitions.notes: Effector mechanisms: Cytokine release (IFN-γ, TNF) and direct cytotoxic killing (perforin/granzyme, Fas/FasL).

definitions.definition: The branch of adaptive immunity mediated by B lymphocytes and the soluble antibodies (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE) they secrete into extracellular fluids, blood, and lymph to eliminate extracellular pathogens and neutralize toxins.
definitions.notes: Effector mechanisms: Neutralization, opsonization, complement activation, and ADCC.

definitions.definition: A state of antigen-specific non-responsiveness or unresponsiveness by the immune system induced by prior exposure to that specific antigen. It is essential for preventing autoimmune attacks against the host's own self-antigens.
definitions.notes: Maintained through Central Tolerance (thymic/bone marrow deletion) and Peripheral Tolerance (anergy, regulatory T cells / Tregs).

definitions.definition: An inappropriate, excessive, or exaggerated adaptive immune response upon secondary or repeated exposure to an antigen (allergen), resulting in tissue damage, inflammation, or functional impairment.
definitions.notes: Gell & Coombs classification: Type I (IgE Immediate), Type II (Cytotoxic IgG/IgM), Type III (Immune Complex), Type IV (Delayed T-cell mediated).

definitions.definition: An in vitro serological diagnostic reaction where particulate antigens (such as whole bacteria or red blood cells) or soluble antigens coated onto carrier particles combine with specific bivalent antibodies, forming visible clumps or aggregates.
definitions.notes: Used in ABO blood typing, Widal test (typhoid), and cross-matching.

definitions.definition: A highly sensitive, quantitative serological technique that utilizes enzyme-linked antibodies or antigens to detect and quantify the presence of specific antigens or antibodies in clinical samples via a colorimetric enzyme-substrate reaction.
definitions.notes: Formats: Direct, Indirect (HIV antibody screening), and Sandwich ELISA.

definitions.definition: A biological preparation of weakened, killed, or subunit components of a microorganism (or mRNA encoding microbial antigens) administered to induce active adaptive immunity and protective immunological memory without causing severe clinical disease.
definitions.notes: Types: Live-attenuated (MMR, BCG, Polio Sabin), Inactivated (Rabies, Salk Polio), Toxoids (Tetanus, Diphtheria), Recombinant Subunit (Hepatitis B), and mRNA vaccines.

definitions.definition: The induction of immunity by stimulating the host's own immune system to produce antibodies and sensitized memory lymphocytes through natural infection or artificial vaccination.
definitions.notes: Onset is delayed (takes 1–2 weeks), but confers long-lasting protection (years to lifetime memory).

definitions.definition: The acquisition of temporary immunity through the transfer of pre-formed antibodies from another individual or animal.
definitions.notes: Natural: Maternal IgG across placenta, sIgA in breast milk. Artificial: Antivenom, tetanus antitoxin (TAT), rabies immunoglobulin (RIG). Immediate onset, but short duration (weeks/months).

questions.title: Functions of the Immune System
questions.question: What are the core physiological functions of the human immune system?
questions.summary: The immune system maintains homeostasis through 4 fundamental pillars: Defense, Clearance, Surveillance, and Immune Tolerance.

sections.heading: 1. Defense Against Pathogens (Immune Defense)
sections.content: Identifies and destroys disease-causing foreign invaders (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites). Hyperactivity causes hypersensitivity/allergy; deficiency causes immunodeficiency and recurrent infections.

sections.heading: 2. Clearance and Tissue Repair (Immune Homeostasis)
sections.content: Initiates controlled inflammation to remove aging, damaged, or apoptotic host cells and eliminates circulating immune complexes to begin tissue healing.

sections.heading: 3. Immune Surveillance
sections.content: Continuously monitors the body to detect and directly destroy mutated, abnormal endogenous cells such as virus-infected cells and tumor cells.

sections.heading: 4. Immune Tolerance
sections.content: Actively distinguishes 'self' from 'non-self', mounting strong attacks against foreign threats while remaining strictly unresponsive to healthy host tissues. Breakdown leads to autoimmune diseases.

questions.title: Differences between T-Cell and B-Cell Epitopes
questions.question: Compare the key differences between T-cell epitopes and B-cell epitopes.
questions.summary: T-cell epitopes are internal linear peptides presented on MHC molecules, whereas B-cell epitopes are accessible surface conformational structures recognized in their native state.

rows: Binds to BCR on B-cells or soluble antibodies
Requires APC processing and presentation on MHC I or II
No APC processing or MHC presentation required

questions.title: Differences between Thymus-Dependent (TD-Ag) and Thymus-Independent (TI-Ag) Antigens
questions.question: Differentiate between Thymus-Dependent Antigens (TD-Ag) and Thymus-Independent Antigens (TI-Ag).
questions.summary: TD antigens require T-cell help to activate B cells and induce class switching & high-affinity memory, while TI antigens activate B cells directly without T-cell help.

questions.title: Molecular Structure and Biological Functions of Immunoglobulins (Antibodies)
questions.question: Describe the four-chain basic structure and biological functions of Immunoglobulin (antibody) molecules.
questions.summary: Antibodies consist of 2 Heavy (H) and 2 Light (L) chains with variable (Fab) and constant (Fc) regions performing antigen neutralization, opsonization, complement activation, and ADCC.

sections.heading: 1. Molecular Structure
sections.content:
• Basic Core: Y-shaped molecule made of 4 polypeptide chains: 2 identical Heavy (H) chains and 2 identical Light (L) chains joined by disulfide bonds.
• Variable (V) Region / Fab: The tips of the arms. Contains Hypervariable Regions (HVR) / CDRs that determine specific antigen binding.
• Constant (C) Region / Fc: The stem. Determines antibody class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE) and contains binding sites for complement C1q and Fc receptors on phagocytes/NK cells.

sections.heading: 2. Biological Functions
sections.content:
• Neutralization: Binds directly to pathogens or toxins, physically blocking host cell entry.
• Opsonization: Coats pathogens to enhance phagocytosis by macrophages and neutrophils.
• Complement Activation: Antigen-bound IgG/IgM activates C1 to assemble the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC).
• ADCC: Recruits NK cells via CD16/FcγR to lyse antibody-coated infected/tumor cells.
• Specialized Class Roles: IgG crosses placenta (fetal immunity), sIgA protects mucosal surfaces, and IgE mediates allergic/parasitic defense.

questions.title: Hydrolytic Fragments of Immunoglobulins (Papain vs. Pepsin Cleavage)
questions.question: Please state the cleavage sites and hydrolytic fragments of Immunoglobulins (Ig).
questions.summary: Papain cleaves above the hinge yielding 2 Fab + 1 Fc; Pepsin cleaves below the hinge yielding 1 F(ab')2 + degraded pFc' fragments.

sections.heading: 1. Papain Hydrolysis
sections.content:
• Mechanism: Cleaves the antibody molecule above the hinge region.
• Resulting Fragments: Yields 3 fragments: Two Fab (Fragment antigen-binding) fragments (each monovalent) and one Fc (Fragment crystallizable) fragment.

sections.heading: 2. Pepsin Hydrolysis
sections.content:
• Mechanism: Cleaves the antibody molecule below the disulfide bonds in the heavy chain hinge region.
• Resulting Fragments: Yields one large F(ab')2 fragment (bivalent, keeps two antigen-binding sites connected) and smaller pFc' peptide fragments.

questions.title: Three Activation Pathways of the Complement System
questions.question: Compare the three activation pathways of the complement system.
questions.summary: Classical, Alternative, and Lectin pathways differ in activators and convertases but converge to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC).

rows: MBL binding to mannose via MASP
C3 tickover, Factor B, Factor D

questions.title: Biological Functions of the Complement System
questions.question: What are the major biological functions of the complement system?
questions.summary: Complement executes cytolysis via MAC pore formation, opsonization for phagocytes, inflammatory recruitment via anaphylatoxins, and immune complex clearance.

sections.heading: 1. Cell Lysis (Cytolysis / MAC Formation)
sections.content: The cascade ends in assembly of the Membrane Attack Complex (C5b-9), puncturing 10-nm pores in target bacterial and cellular membranes, causing osmotic swelling and burst.

sections.heading: 2. Opsonization
sections.content: Fragments C3b and C4b coat pathogen surfaces, binding CR1 receptors on macrophages and neutrophils to massively enhance phagocytosis.

sections.heading: 3. Inflammation & Chemotaxis (Anaphylatoxins)
sections.content: Cleavage peptides C3a, C4a, and C5a act as anaphylatoxins, triggering mast cell degranulation (histamine release, vasodilation). C5a is a potent chemoattractant for neutrophils.

sections.heading: 4. Clearance of Immune Complexes
sections.content: C3b binding to circulating Ag-Ab complexes allows RBCs to carry them to the spleen and liver for destruction by macrophages.

questions.title: General Properties and Biological Functions of Cytokines
questions.question: Describe the general properties, action characteristics, and biological functions of cytokines.
questions.summary: Cytokines are potent, low-molecular-weight proteins that regulate innate and adaptive immunity, hematopoiesis, and inflammation.

sections.heading: 1. General Properties & Characteristics
sections.content:
• Structure: Soluble proteins or polypeptides (8–30 kDa) secreted by immune cells.
• Potency & Range: Extremely potent at picomolar levels; short half-life.
• Modes of Action: Autocrine (self), Paracrine (nearby), Endocrine (distant).
• Action Features: Pleiotropy (one cytokine -> multiple cell types), Redundancy (multiple cytokines -> same effect), Synergy (cooperation), Antagonism (mutual inhibition).

sections.heading: 2. Biological Functions
sections.content:
• Regulate Innate Immunity: Activates macrophages, neutrophils, and NK cells (IFN-α/β, IL-12, TNF-α).
• Regulate Adaptive Immunity: Stimulates T and B cell proliferation and differentiation (IL-2, IL-4, IFN-γ).
• Mediate Inflammation: Pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α) induce fever and tissue inflammation.
• Stimulate Hematopoiesis: Drives bone marrow stem cell differentiation (CSFs, IL-3, EPO).
• Anti-Infection & Anti-Tumor: IFNs block viral replication; TNF induces tumor apoptosis.

questions.title: Mechanism of CTL-Mediated Killing of Target Cells
questions.question: Explain the mechanisms by which CD8+ Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (CTLs) kill infected or abnormal target cells.
questions.summary: CTLs kill target cells via the Perforin/Granzyme pathway and the Fas/FasL death receptor pathway.

sections.heading: 1. Perforin and Granzyme Pathway
sections.content:
• Perforin: Drills physical pores into the target cell membrane.
• Granzymes: Enter the target cell through perforin pores, cleaving and activating caspases (caspase cascade) to directly trigger apoptotic cell death.

sections.heading: 2. Fas and FasL Pathway
sections.content:
• Activated CTLs express Fas Ligand (FasL / CD95L) on their surface.
• FasL binds to the Fas receptor (CD95) on the target cell, activating intracellular death domains and caspases, inducing target cell apoptosis.

questions.title: Biological Functions of CD4+ Th1 Cells and CD4+ Th2 Cells
questions.question: Compare the differentiating cytokines, secreted effector molecules, and biological functions of CD4+ Th1 and CD4+ Th2 cells.
questions.summary: Th1 cells drive cellular immunity against intracellular pathogens, whereas Th2 cells drive humoral immunity, eosinophil activation, and allergy against extracellular parasites.

rows: Stimulates B-cell class switching to IgG/IgA/IgE

questions.title: Characteristics of Primary and Secondary Humoral Immune Response
questions.question: Compare the primary and secondary antibody responses following antigen exposure.
questions.summary: Secondary immune responses feature a shorter lag phase, higher antibody titer, predominantly IgG isotype, higher affinity, and longer duration due to memory B cells.

rows: Predominantly IgM first, followed by IgG

questions.title: Antigen Presenting Pathways (Endogenous vs. Exogenous Pathways)
questions.question: Compare the Endogenous (MHC-I) and Exogenous (MHC-II) antigen presentation pathways.
questions.summary: Endogenous pathway processes cytosolic viral/tumor antigens via proteasomes to MHC-I for CD8+ T cells; Exogenous pathway processes engulfed extracellular antigens via endosomes to MHC-II for CD4+ T cells.

rows: MHC Class I -> CD8+ Cytotoxic T Cells
MHC Class II -> CD4+ Helper T Cells

questions.title: Differences between MHC-I and MHC-II Molecules
questions.question: Compare MHC Class I and MHC Class II molecules.
questions.summary: MHC I is found on all nucleated cells presenting to CD8+ CTLs; MHC II is restricted to professional APCs presenting to CD4+ Th cells.

α chain (34 kDa) + β chain (29 kDa)
Formed by α1 and α2 domains (closed ends, 8–10 aa)

questions.title: Biological Functions of MHC Molecules
questions.question: What are the primary biological and clinical functions of MHC molecules?
questions.summary: MHC molecules control antigen presentation, guide T cell maturation in thymus, restrict immune responses, and determine graft histocompatibility.

sections.heading: 1. Antigen Presentation & T-Cell Activation
sections.content: MHC molecules bind peptide fragments and display them on cell surfaces. TCRs can only recognize antigens when presented bound to self-MHC (MHC Restriction).

sections.heading: 2. Regulation of Thymic T-Cell Maturation
sections.content: MHC molecules in the thymus mediate Positive Selection (ensuring self-MHC recognition) and Negative Selection (deleting autoreactive clones for central tolerance).

sections.heading: 3. Determining Genetic Susceptibility to Diseases
sections.content: Certain HLA alleles are strongly associated with specific autoimmune disorders (e.g. HLA-B27 with Ankylosing Spondylitis, HLA-DR4 with Rheumatoid Arthritis).

sections.heading: 4. Regulating Allograft Rejection
sections.content: MHC differences between donor and recipient are the primary antigens that trigger allograft transplant rejection.

questions.title: Role of Primary vs. Secondary Lymphoid Organs
questions.question: Compare the anatomical roles of Primary (Central) and Secondary (Peripheral) Lymphoid Organs.
questions.summary: Primary organs (Bone Marrow, Thymus) generate and educate immune cells; Secondary organs (Lymph Nodes, Spleen, MALT) trap antigens and initiate adaptive immune responses.

rows: Lymph Nodes, Spleen, Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT)
Origin, differentiation, and maturation of B and T lymphocytes
Antigen capture, lymphocyte activation, and immune response execution

questions.title: Dual Signal Model of T-Cell Activation
questions.question: Explain the activation signals required for full activation of naive T lymphocytes.
questions.summary: T-cell activation strictly requires 2 signals: Signal 1 (Antigen recognition) and Signal 2 (Co-stimulation); without Signal 2, the cell enters anergy.

sections.heading: 1. Signal 1 (Specific Antigen Signal)
sections.content: TCR binds specifically to peptide-MHC complex on APC, assisted by CD4 or CD8 co-receptors and transduced via CD3 complex.

sections.heading: 2. Signal 2 (Co-stimulatory Signal)
sections.content: CD28 on T cell binds to CD80 (B7-1) or CD86 (B7-2) on APC. Essential for IL-2 secretion and clonal expansion. (Signal 1 alone without Signal 2 induces T-cell anergy/inactivation).

sections.heading: 3. Signal 3 (Cytokine Differentiation Signal)
sections.content: Cytokines secreted by APCs (such as IL-12 for Th1, IL-4 for Th2, IL-6/TGF-β for Th17) direct the differentiation into specific effector T-cell lineages.

questions.title: Activation Signals Required for B-Cell Activation
questions.question: Explain the activation signals required for full activation and antibody production by B lymphocytes.
questions.summary: B-cell activation for TD antigens requires BCR antigen cross-linking (Signal 1), CD40-CD40L interaction with helper T cells (Signal 2), and cytokines (IL-4, IL-5) for class switching.

sections.heading: 1. Signal 1 (Antigen Recognition)
sections.content: Membrane-bound BCR (mIgM/mIgD) binds directly to intact conformational epitope on antigen, transducing signals via Igα/Igβ (CD79a/CD79b).

sections.heading: 2. Signal 2 (T-Cell Help / Co-stimulation)
sections.content: CD40 on B cell binds to CD40 Ligand (CD40L / CD154) on activated CD4+ Helper T cells. Essential for germinal center formation and somatic hypermutation.

sections.heading: 3. Signal 3 (Cytokines)
sections.content: Helper T-cell cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IL-21) drive B-cell proliferation, isotype class switching (IgM -> IgG/IgA/IgE), and differentiation into plasma and memory cells.

questions.title: Biological Functions of Natural Killer (NK) Cells
questions.question: What are the biological functions and target cell recognition mechanisms of Natural Killer (NK) cells?
questions.summary: NK cells provide rapid innate surveillance against virus-infected and tumor cells via 'Missing-Self' recognition and ADCC without prior sensitization.

sections.heading: 1. Direct Cytotoxicity (Missing-Self Recognition)
sections.content:
• Killer Activation Receptors (KAR) recognize stress ligands on abnormal cells.
• Killer Inhibitory Receptors (KIR) bind normal self-MHC Class I.
• If target cell downregulates MHC-I (viral evasion or tumor mutation), KIR is not engaged, and NK cells release perforin/granzymes to kill the target ('Missing-Self' hypothesis).

sections.heading: 2. Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC)
sections.content: NK cells express CD16 (FcγRIII) which binds to IgG antibodies coating target cells, triggering targeted cytotoxic degranulation.

sections.heading: 3. Immunoregulatory Cytokine Production
sections.content: NK cells rapidly secrete large amounts of IFN-γ and TNF-α upon activation, promoting macrophage activation and Th1 polarization.

questions.title: Main Characteristics and Biological Functions of Macrophages
questions.question: Describe the major biological functions and immune roles of Macrophages.
questions.summary: Macrophages act as professional phagocytes, antigen-presenting cells, inflammatory cytokine producers, and tissue repair coordinators.

sections.heading: 1. Phagocytosis & Pathogen Destruction
sections.content: Engulfs bacteria and debris using PRRs, opsonins (C3b, IgG), and destroys invaders via Oxygen-Dependent (Respiratory Burst, ROS, NO) and Oxygen-Independent (lysosomal enzymes, defensins) pathways.

sections.heading: 2. Professional Antigen Presentation (APC)
sections.content: Degrades exogenous protein antigens in endolysosomes and presents peptide fragments on MHC Class II molecules with co-stimulatory molecules (CD80/CD86) to activate CD4+ T cells.

sections.heading: 3. Cytokine & Inflammatory Mediator Secretion
sections.content: Produces pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12) and chemokines (IL-8) to recruit leukocytes and initiate systemic acute-phase responses.

sections.heading: 4. Tissue Repair and Remodeling
sections.content: Clears apoptotic cells and secretes growth factors (VEGF, TGF-β, FGF) that stimulate angiogenesis and wound healing.

questions.title: Classification and Distinct Characteristics of the 5 Immunoglobulin Classes
questions.question: Describe the structure, distribution, and clinical significance of the 5 immunoglobulin isotypes (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE).
questions.summary: IgG is the main serum antibody crossing placenta; IgA protects mucosa; IgM is the primary pentameric responder; IgE mediates allergies; IgD is a naive B-cell receptor.

rows: Predominant antibody in secondary response; only isotype that crosses the placenta; fixes complement, opsonizes, and mediates ADCC.
Main antibody in external mucosal secretions (colostrum, saliva, gut, tears); prevents mucosal microbial adhesion.
Pentamer with J-chain (or monomer on naive B cell)
First antibody produced in primary immune response; most efficient complement activator (due to 10 antigen-binding sites); natural isohemagglutinins (anti-A, anti-B).
Expressed with IgM on mature naive B cells; serves as a membrane antigen receptor for B-cell differentiation.
Binds high-affinity FcεRI on mast cells and basophils; mediates Type I immediate hypersensitivity (allergy) and defense against parasitic helminths.

questions.title: Mechanisms of Immune Tolerance (Central vs. Peripheral Tolerance)
questions.question: Explain the central and peripheral mechanisms that maintain immunological self-tolerance.
questions.summary: Central tolerance eliminates autoreactive clones in primary organs (thymus/bone marrow); peripheral tolerance controls escaped autoreactive cells via anergy, suppression, and deletion.

sections.heading: 1. Central Tolerance (Thymus & Bone Marrow)
sections.content:
• Clonal Deletion (Negative Selection): Developing T cells in thymic medulla and B cells in bone marrow that bind strongly to self-antigens undergo apoptosis.
• Receptor Editing: Autoreactive immature B cells can rearrange light chain genes (κ/λ) to generate non-autoreactive BCRs.
• AIRE Gene Function: Autoimmune Regulator (AIRE) drives expression of tissue-restricted peripheral self-antigens in thymic medullary epithelial cells.

sections.heading: 2. Peripheral Tolerance (Secondary Organs & Tissues)
sections.content:
• Clonal Anergy: Functional inactivation of autoreactive T cells when recognizing antigen without co-stimulation (Signal 1 without Signal 2).
• Regulatory T Cells (Tregs / CD4+CD25+FoxP3+): Actively suppress autoreactive T cells via inhibitory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) and CTLA-4.
• Immune Privileged Sites: Blood-brain barrier, eye, testis, and placenta limit immune entry and express FasL to induce apoptosis in attacking lymphocytes.

questions.title: Types of Vaccines and Artificial Immunization
questions.question: Classify the major types of vaccines used in clinical immunization, citing examples and advantages/disadvantages.
questions.summary: Vaccines simulate infection to establish immunological memory; categories include live-attenuated, inactivated, toxoid, subunit, and mRNA vaccines.

sections.heading: 1. Live-Attenuated Vaccines
sections.content:
• Characteristics: Microbes weakened so they replicate without causing severe illness. Induces strong cellular (CTL) and humoral immunity with lifelong protection.
• Examples: MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella), BCG (Tuberculosis), Oral Polio (Sabin), Yellow fever, Varicella.
• Caution: Contraindicated in immunocompromised individuals and pregnant women.

sections.heading: 2. Inactivated (Killed) Vaccines
sections.content:
• Characteristics: Microbes killed by chemicals or heat. Cannot replicate; extremely safe but usually requires booster doses and adjuvants to maintain immunity.
• Examples: Inactivated Polio (Salk), Rabies, Hepatitis A, Whole-cell Pertussis.

sections.heading: 3. Toxoids
sections.content:
• Characteristics: Inactivated bacterial exotoxins that retain immunogenicity but lose toxicity.
• Examples: Tetanus toxoid (TT), Diphtheria toxoid (DT).

sections.heading: 4. Subunit & Recombinant Vaccines
sections.content:
• Characteristics: Purified specific antigenic fragments (capsular polysaccharides or recombinant viral surface proteins).
• Examples: Hepatitis B vaccine (HBsAg produced in yeast), HPV vaccine (virus-like particles), Pneumococcal conjugate.

questions.title: Classification of Antigens (By Source, T-Dependence, and Immunogenicity)
questions.question: How are antigens classified based on their relationship with the host, dependence on T cells, and immunogenicity?
questions.summary: Antigens are classified by T-cell dependence (TD vs TI), origin/relationship (Xeno-, Allo-, Auto-, Heterophilic), and immunogenicity (Complete vs Hapten).

sections.heading: 1. Based on Dependence on T Cells
sections.content:
• Thymus-Dependent Antigens (TD-Ag): Proteins requiring T-cell help for B-cell activation, class switching, and memory.
• Thymus-Independent Antigens (TI-Ag): Polysaccharides with repeating units that activate B cells directly without T-cell help (mostly IgM, no memory).

sections.heading: 2. Based on Relationship with the Host (Source)
sections.content:
• Xenogenic Antigen (Xenoantigen): Antigens originating from an entirely different species.
• Allogenic Antigen (Alloantigen): Antigens from genetically different individuals of the same species (ABO blood groups, HLA).
• Autoantigen: Host's own normal tissue antigens that mistakenly induce an autoimmune response.
• Heterophilic Antigen (Forssman Ag): Common antigens shared across unrelated species (human, sheep RBCs, microbes).

sections.heading: 3. Based on Immunogenicity
sections.content:
• Complete Antigen: Possesses both immunogenicity and immunoreactivity.
• Incomplete Antigen (Hapten): Has immunoreactivity alone; becomes immunogenic only when conjugated to a carrier protein.

questions.title: Definition and Classification of Hypersensitivity Reactions
questions.question: Define Hypersensitivity and list the Gell and Coombs classification of hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.summary: Hypersensitivity is an exaggerated, tissue-damaging immune response upon re-exposure to antigen; classified into Types I, II, III, and IV.

sections.heading: Definition of Hypersensitivity
sections.content: A harmful immune response that occurs when a sensitized (primed) host encounters the exact same antigen for a second time, resulting in exaggerated reactivity that causes tissue injury, inflammation, or functional disorder.

sections.heading: Four-Type Classification (Gell & Coombs)
sections.content:
• Type I: Immediate (IgE-mediated) Hypersensitivity
• Type II: Cytotoxic / Antibody-mediated (IgG/IgM) Hypersensitivity
• Type III: Immune Complex-mediated (Ag-Ab complexes) Hypersensitivity
• Type IV: Cell-mediated or Delayed-Type (T-cell mediated) Hypersensitivity (DTH)

questions.title: Main Features of the Four Types of Hypersensitivity Reactions
questions.question: What are the distinguishing features (mediators, targets, timing, hallmarks) of the four types of hypersensitivity?
questions.summary: Type I is rapid IgE functional disorder; Type II is IgG/IgM cell lysis; Type III is immune complex vasculitis; Type IV is delayed T-cell macrophage inflammation.

rows: IgE antibodies, Mast cells, Basophils, Histamine
Intense functional disorder (vasodilation, bronchospasm) with minimal tissue injury
IgG or IgM antibodies, Complement (MAC), Phagocytes, NK cells
Direct cell lysis, phagocytosis, or tissue destruction
IgG, IgM, Soluble Ag-Ab complexes, Complement (C3a/C5a), Neutrophils
Immune complex deposition in vessel walls causing acute necrotizing vasculitis
Sensitized CD4+ Th1 & CD8+ T cells, Macrophages (No antibodies)
Mononuclear infiltration, granuloma formation, and chronic tissue necrosis

questions.title: Mechanisms Involved in Each Type of Hypersensitivity Reaction
questions.question: Describe the step-by-step immunological mechanisms for each type of hypersensitivity reaction.
questions.summary: Type I crosslinks IgE; Type II activates complement/opsonization/ADCC; Type III deposits complexes recruiting neutrophils; Type IV releases Th1 cytokines activating macrophages.

sections.heading: 1. Type I (Immediate) Mechanism
sections.content:
• Initial Exposure: Allergen induces B cells to produce IgE, which binds via Fc to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils (sensitization).
• Re-exposure: Allergen cross-links bound IgE, triggering rapid degranulation: preformed mediators (histamine, ECF-A) in early phase (minutes) and synthesized mediators (leukotrienes, PGD2) in late phase (hours).

sections.heading: 2. Type II (Cytotoxic) Mechanism
sections.content:
• IgG/IgM binds directly to antigens on target cell surfaces.
• Cell destruction occurs via 3 pathways: (1) Complement activation (MAC lysis), (2) Opsonization (C3b/IgG binding phagocyte receptors), and (3) ADCC (NK cells releasing perforin/granzyme via FcγRIII).

sections.heading: 3. Type III (Immune Complex) Mechanism
sections.content:
• Soluble antigens bind antibodies forming medium-sized circulating complexes that escape phagocytic clearance and deposit on vascular basement membranes.
• Complexes activate complement (C3a, C5a), recruiting neutrophils that release lysosomal enzymes and reactive oxygen species, destroying blood vessel walls (vasculitis).

sections.heading: 4. Type IV (Cell-Mediated) Mechanism
sections.content:
• Sensitized CD4+ Th1 cells recognize antigen presented on APCs and secrete cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2).
• Cytokines recruit and hyperactivate macrophages and CTLs, which release lysosomal proteases and perforin causing delayed, chronic tissue damage (24–72h peak).

questions.title: Common Clinical Diseases Associated with the Four Types of Hypersensitivity
questions.question: List the common clinical diseases associated with each of the four types of hypersensitivity reactions.
questions.summary: Type I includes anaphylaxis and asthma; Type II includes hemolytic anemia and transfusion reactions; Type III includes SLE and serum sickness; Type IV includes contact dermatitis and TB granulomas.

sections.heading: 1. Type I (Immediate) Clinical Diseases
sections.content:
• Systemic Anaphylaxis: Anaphylactic shock from penicillin, bee stings, or foreign serums.
• Respiratory: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) and allergic extrinsic asthma.
• Gastrointestinal: Food allergies (peanuts, shellfish, milk, eggs).
• Cutaneous: Acute urticaria (hives) and atopic eczema.

sections.heading: 2. Type II (Cytotoxic) Clinical Diseases
sections.content:
• Transfusion Reactions: ABO incompatibility acute hemolytic transfusion reactions.
• Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn: Erythroblastosis fetalis (Rh incompatibility).
• Drug-Induced Hemolytic Anemia: Penicillin/quinidine coating RBCs.
• Autoimmune Conditions: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome, Myasthenia gravis, Graves' disease, Pemphigus vulgaris.

sections.heading: 3. Type III (Immune Complex) Clinical Diseases
sections.content:
• Localized: Arthus reaction (localized cutaneous vasculitis and necrosis).
• Systemic: Serum sickness (fever, rash, arthritis following foreign serum/antivenom injection).
• Autoimmune & Post-Infectious: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE lupus nephritis), Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).

sections.heading: 4. Type IV (Delayed-Type) Clinical Diseases
sections.content:
• Contact Dermatitis: Poison ivy (urushiol), nickel jewelry, cosmetics, topical medications.
• Diagnostic Tests: Tuberculin PPD skin test reaction (Mantoux test for TB exposure).
• Granulomatous Infections: Caseating granulomas in Tuberculosis (TB) and Leprosy.
• Transplant Pathology: Acute and chronic cellular allograft rejection.
